title: Shallow Quantum Circuits for Geometrically Local Lindblad Dynamics
authors: Zheyu Shen, Yusen Wu, Xiao Yuan, Yukun Zhang
abstract: Open-system dynamics govern decoherence, transport, and engineered dissipation in quantum many-body systems. We propose a quantum algorithm for simulating time-independent, finite-range Lindblad dynamics with bounded local strength on a constant-dimensional lattice of $n$ sites, allowing noncommuting jump operators. For time $T\ge1$ and diamond-norm error at most $ε$, it has depth $O(T\operatorname{polylog}(nT/ε))$ and gate count $O(nT\operatorname{polylog}(nT/ε))$. These results extend the HHKL spatial decomposition to open systems. The main obstacle is that the reversible overlap corrections used for unitary dynamics have no direct analogue for dissipative channels. We overcome this by retaining the environment in a shared unitary dilation, keeping information lost from the system coherently available and making the spatial corrections reversible. We prove exponential occupation bounds for the environmental states generated by the decomposition, allowing compact representation and coherent simulation of local factors on the inputs that arise. The construction reduces each short-time evolution to a constant number of parallel layers on regions of logarithmic diameter, using nearest-neighbour gates and polylogarithmic auxiliary density.   We also prove unconditional worst-case lower bounds using time-independent, purely dissipative processes that transport quantum information. For circuits with local quantum and classical communication, the lower bounds are $Ω(nT)$ for the expected gate count and $Ω(T)$ for depth on time scales up to the lattice diameter. They match the upper bounds' leading time and volume dependence up to polylogarithmic factors. At fixed time and sufficiently small fixed error, we further prove a depth lower bound of $Ω(\log n/\log\log n)$, showing that global accuracy can require increasing depth as the lattice grows.
summary: This paper presents a quantum algorithm to simulate open-system dynamics governed by Lindblad equations on a lattice. By employing a shared unitary dilation to manage environmental information, the authors achieve resource scaling for gate count and depth that matches the best known bounds for unitary evolution. This advances the field by providing efficient quantum simulation tools for dissipative quantum many-body systems.
main_problem: The paper addresses the challenge of simulating open-system dynamics governed by Lindblad operators using quantum circuits.
main_result: They propose an algorithm achieving resource scaling matching Hamiltonian simulation, providing both upper bounds (gate count and depth) and matching lower bounds for time-independent, finite-range Lindblad dynamics.
method: The core method involves using a common unitary dilation to handle the environment, circumventing the lack of reversible overlap corrections for dissipative channels, and employing techniques like dyadic factorization.
model_or_system: The model is an open quantum system on a constant-dimensional lattice of $n$ sites, whose evolution is described by a Lindblad master equation involving local Hermitian Hamiltonians and noncommuting jump operators.
key_observables: Gate count, circuit depth, and the fidelity of the simulation relative to the error tolerance $\epsilon$.
important_parameters: Time $T$, lattice size $n$, error $\epsilon$, and the local strength of the dissipation.
main_assumptions: The construction relies on proving exponential occupation bounds for environmental states and assumes the use of a shared unitary dilation.
figures_summary: No specific figures were summarized, but the notes detail complexity bounds for gate count and depth.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the problem, details the unitary dilation and decomposition techniques, presents the complexity upper bounds (Theorem 1.1), and concludes with matching lower bounds derived from purely dissipative processes.
why_interesting: This work provides a rigorous, resource-efficient quantum algorithm for simulating dissipative processes, which is crucial for modeling realistic quantum devices where decoherence is dominant.

Figure 4: Four-leaf input tree, with occurrence indices 1, . . . , 4 encoded as addresses 00, 01, 10, 11. Each node rotates its two child representatives; the orthogonal coordinates remain present. All rotations are in the private Q = 0 sector and are controlled by the bath configuration after Q. The inverse output tree has the same pairs in reverse level order, with the transposed OAB rotations instead of IAB. The edges describe the recursion, not physical data movement.
